Think of the word "savoury" — it describes something pleasant, appealing, and wholesome (originally, something that tastes or smells good). Now add "un-" to the front, and you get the opposite: something that is unpleasant, off-putting, or morally distasteful.

The simplest way to remember it: if something is unsavoury, it makes a decent, reasonable person feel uncomfortable, uneasy, or disgusted — either in a physical sense (rare) or, far more commonly, in a moral or social sense.

Meaning 1 — Literal: Unpleasant in Taste or Smell

In its original, physical sense, "unsavoury" describes food or drink that smells or tastes unpleasant or off-putting.

"The soup had an unsavoury odour, so nobody touched it."

This usage is quite rare in modern everyday English. When people want to say food smells or tastes bad, they usually just say "bad," "off," or "disgusting." You might encounter this literal meaning in older writing or formal descriptions.

Meaning 2 — Figurative: Morally or Socially Distasteful (This is the main, everyday meaning)

This is where the real power and common usage of the word lives. In this figurative sense, "unsavoury" describes anything — a person, a situation, a set of facts, a reputation, or a behaviour — that is morally questionable, socially unacceptable, ethically murky, or simply not clean in character.

When you call something unsavoury in this sense, you're saying: "This doesn't sit right. A decent person would feel uncomfortable with this."

Here is what this looks like across different contexts:

People: An unsavoury person is someone whose character, history, or associations raise red flags. They might not be an outright criminal, but something about them is off — they're dishonest, disreputable, or involved in things that respectable people avoid.

"He was warned to stay away from the unsavoury characters he had been spending time with."

Behaviour or Actions: An unsavoury act is one that crosses ethical or social lines — it might be manipulative, cruel, corrupt, exploitative, or just deeply inappropriate.

"The court heard some unsavoury details about how the business had been run."

Reputations and Histories: A person, place, or organisation can have an unsavoury reputation or an unsavoury past — meaning their history is tainted by wrongdoing, scandal, or association with bad things.

"The club had an unsavoury reputation for violence and illegal activity."

Situations and Deals: An unsavoury situation or deal is one that feels dirty, shady, or morally compromised, even if it isn't technically illegal.

"She wanted nothing to do with the unsavoury arrangement her boss had proposed."

"Unsavoury" sits at a moderate-to-strong level of negativity. Here's how to place it:

  • It is stronger than simply "unpleasant" or "a bit awkward."
  • It is not quite as strong as "corrupt," "criminal," or "evil."
  • It often describes something that hasn't necessarily crossed a legal line, but has clearly crossed a moral or social one.

The word also carries a slightly formal, restrained quality. Saying someone is an "unsavoury character" rather than a "dodgy person" or a "bad guy" is the kind of language you'd find in a newspaper article, a court, formal speech, or careful writing. It's controlled disapproval — the word wrinkles its nose at something rather than shouting at it.

To keep the meaning sharp, here's what the word is not:

  • It does not mean boring, sad, or annoying.
  • It does not necessarily mean illegal (though the subject might be).
  • It does not mean unhealthy or fattening (you would not call a greasy burger "unsavoury" unless it actually smells bad).
  • It is not a mild word. Calling something or someone "unsavoury" is a real criticism with weight behind it.

In real-world English, "unsavoury" is most commonly seen paired with these words:

  • unsavoury characters (the most common pairing)
  • unsavoury reputation / past / history
  • unsavoury details / revelations
  • unsavoury business / dealings / practices
  • unsavoury elements (referring to bad people within a group)
  • unsavoury associations (links to bad people or things)

Learning these pairings will help you recognise and use the word naturally.
Words Close in Meaning (and How They Differ)

• Disreputable — very similar; focuses specifically on a damaged or bad reputation.
  • Shady — more informal and colloquial; implies something hidden or dishonest.
  • Sordid — stronger and darker; often implies something shameful involving scandal, sex, crime, or filth.
  • Distasteful — closely related; emphasises that something offends good taste and decency.
  • Dubious — milder; mainly questions whether something is honest or legitimate.
  • Questionable — the mildest of these; simply suggests something is not clearly above board.

Among these, "unsavoury" is closest in feeling to distasteful and disreputable — formal, controlled, and suggesting something that a decent person would reject or avoid.

If you had to remember just one thing about "unsavoury," remember this: it describes something that offends moral decency or good character — the kind of thing that makes a reasonable person pull back and want no part of it. It's the word you reach for when something or someone has a dirty, questionable, or morally murky quality — not necessarily evil, but certainly not clean.
